title: Victor Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Victor wells have a 300-foot median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $25,500-$42,000.
h1: What Victor, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying mountain property near Victor means planning around fractured bedrock, not assuming a shallow water source. Records within 5 miles show a 300-foot median well depth, a middle half from 140 to 440 feet, and a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for budgeting, but they do not guarantee a result on a particular lot. The records include 590 permitted wells, while only 298 are recorded as constructed. Before buying in Victor, Goldfield, or toward Cripple Creek, review nearby well permits, water levels, geology, septic feasibility, and the intended use of the property.

sections.heading: Victor’s mountain bedrock sets the drilling depth
sections.html:
Victor wells are mainly completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. The records identify fractured granite for 6 wells, and the surrounding geology is typically granite or gneiss. Water comes through fractures, so depth can change sharply from one parcel to the next.

The middle half of reported depths runs from 140 to 440 feet. About 22% are under 100 feet, 28% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 39% run from 300 to 600 feet. Another 11% exceed 600 feet, with the deepest record reaching 3,140 feet. For a drilling bid, use the local range as a planning guide rather than a promise. A median-depth estimate is more useful than assuming every Victor lot needs a shallow well.

sections.heading: How much water Victor wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 151 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces from 2.0 to 9.1 gallons per minute, which is a workable range for many household situations when storage and the well system are properly designed.

Yield is not uniform. About 9% of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, while 32% fall from 1 to 5 gallons per minute. The largest group, 55%, is between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 5% exceed 15 gallons per minute. A result under 1 gallon per minute deserves serious review, but a slower well may still work with adequate storage, subject to the permit and intended use.

sections.heading: Victor water levels show little decade-to-decade change
sections.html:
Only 45 wells report a static water level, so this part of the record is much thinner than the depth data. The median depth to water is 100 feet, with the middle half from 58 to 175 feet below the surface.

The decade figures do not show a strong documented decline. The median was 100 feet below ground in the 2010s and 105 feet in the 2020s. That small difference is not enough to establish a dropping regional water table, especially with the limited number of measurements. On a property you are considering, ask for the well construction report, static level, pumping test information, and any recent observations. Water level, well depth, and pumping yield are different measurements and should not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Victor, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity has continued across several decades. Records show 22 permits from the 1970s, 46 from the 1980s, 140 from the 1990s, 191 from the 2000s, 80 from the 2010s, and 73 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the local data is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Mountain Well Improvement LLC (Wiley, David D.), with 131 records; Authorized (PE, PG), with 127; and Black Mountain Drilling (Schnoes, Adam J.), with 51. These counts describe permit records, not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability. Confirm licensing, scope, insurance, and who will handle the pump, pressure tank, electrical work, and final well paperwork before signing a contract.

sections.heading: What a Victor well may cost to drill and finish
sections.html:
Victor’s fractured granite and gneiss make footage the main cost driver. The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models at about $19,500 to $30,000.

A usable water system costs more than the borehole. Including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled finished-well range is about $25,500 to $42,000 at that median depth. A shallow successful well may cost less, while a deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, or a dry hole can change the final bill. Ask the driller to separate footage, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and contingencies in the estimate.

sections.heading: Victor buyers need to check mines, water quality, and septic layout
sections.html:
There are 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 437 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped within about 10 miles. That does not prove a specific parcel is contaminated, but it is a reason to test the water and research the property’s mining history before closing. A water-quality test should match local concerns and the intended household use.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured mountain rock. Septic setbacks, a suitable soil absorption area, driveway access for a rig, and room for tanks and electrical equipment also affect whether a lot can be developed. Check these items early. A well permit does not by itself establish that a home site, septic system, or proposed use is feasible.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Victor, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Victor is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 140 to 440 feet. About 39% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, while 11% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 3,140 feet, showing how unpredictable fractured mountain bedrock can be.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Victor, Colorado?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 300-foot median depth, drilling the hole models at $19,500 to $30,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical models at $25,500 to $42,000. Access, depth, casing, and a dry hole can change the actual price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Victor, Colorado?
faq.a: Among 151 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 2.0 to 9.1 gallons per minute. About 9% report under 1 gallon per minute. That level may require storage planning and careful household-use review. A nearby well’s yield is evidence for planning, not a guarantee for your parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Victor, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from yield or depth alone. Within about 10 miles, the records map 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 437 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for appropriate contaminants, especially where mining or other site history raises concern, and retest after construction or treatment changes.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well near Victor, Colorado?
faq.a: Possibly, but confirm more than a well permit. Local records are mostly domestic or household wells, at 62% of the use mix, and 0% are identified as Denver Basin aquifer wells. Check the DWR permit, available yield, water quality, septic soils and setbacks, driveway access, and building-site layout. A low-yield well may require storage planning.
